catalog_quote: [p.26, 2.4.3] Although on the surface, stress appears to be phonemic, it is predictable at this underlying level of analysis. There is a rule that predominantly assigns antepenultimate stress, operating from the word boundary. There are certain circumstances in which stress is retracted or advanced in the word. To account for these shifts of stress it is necessary to speak in terms of underlying 'unstressable' vowels ... [p.29, 2.6.1] The effect of this rule is to apply stress to the antepenultimate syllable in most cases ... The first part of this rule states that stress is assigned to: (i) The antepenultimate syllable of a word of three or more syllables when this is not marked with the feature [+unstressable] or when it is not morpheme final. audit.reasoning: The classification (antepenultimate default from the right word edge; initial=penultimate in disyllables; lexically conditioned pre-antepenultimate/penultimate via [unstressable] vowels; no secondary stress described) rests on Crowley 1982, the standard 268-pp reference grammar by the language's principal describer, held with a text; every deciding quotation was re-located verbatim at the cited pages (19, 26, 27-28, 29, 31). Glottolog lists no phonology-specific work and no later grammar; Crowley's 1992 dictionary (downloaded, open) defers to the 1982 phonology and marks no stress; the one stress-specific article found (Lee 1999, downloaded, open, scanned) re-derives exactly our pattern from Crowley's data and states there is no secondary stress. StressTyp2's simpler statement is a Hayes-1995-mediated simplification of the same source, already flagged in the record. No better or contradicting sour

sources.citation: Lee, Minkyung. 1999. An Optimality Theoretic analysis of Paamese stress. Kansas Working Papers in Linguistics 24(1):59-80. doi:10.17161/kwpl.1808.354
sources.quote: p.59: 'In Paamese, stress typically falls on the antepenultimate syllable in words with three or more syllables while stress goes on the pre-antepenultimate position if the antepenultimate vowel is unstressable. In disyllabic words, stress goes to the penultimate syllable, i.e. the initial syllable. Penultimate stress is also observed in trisyllabic words when the initial syllable has an unstressable vowel.' p.61: 'all data hereafter are excerpted from Crowley (1982)'; 'based on the observation that Paamese does not have secondary stress, the alignment constraint All-Ft-R is posited'; fn.2: fi
sources.locator: p.59 (introduction), p.61 (sec.2.1 and fn.2-3); scanned text in PDF has no text)
sources.note: Only stress-specific paper on Paamese (OT reanalysis of Crowley 1982 data); explicitly states no secondary stress, supporting our the secondary-stress rule; now obtained.

sources.citation: Crowley, Terry. 1992. A dictionary of Paamese. Pacific Linguistics C-121. Canberra: ANU. xxi+256 pp.
sources.quote: No stress statement. p.vii: 'The relationship of this orthography to the phonological system of the language is described in Crowley (1982:12-19). The only additional point ... distinctive vowel length ... is systematically marked by a macron'; p.viii refers morphophonological rules to 'Crowley (1982:28-43)'. Headwords and bracketed underlying forms carry no stress or [unstressable] marking (e.g. p.153 tabos [tabose] 'inept' and tahos [tahosi] 'good', the grammar's stress subminimal pair, are unmarked).
sources.locator: General Introduction sec.1 Orthography p.vii; sec.2 p.viii; sample entries p.153
